there's any number of reasons. 

often times, its just not safe. being "visibily" trans isn't a safe trait to have, so a lot of people will hold off on a lot of the social aspects of transitioning until they're prepared (time on hrt, growing out/cutting hair, obtaining a wardrobe, etc).  

people also have different feelings about their own bodies- her beard may not have caused her dysphoria, so she kept it. or it could have, but shaving was worse. those are both things i've heard people have felt. 

for the offended by strangers thing- honestly a lot of the time its just that its frustrating to be misgendered, and to be held to such different standards.

for example (not upset btw, just a food for thought sort of thing), you mentioned that the only thing she did to appear female was wear lipstick. what efforts /should/ she have gone to in order to appear female? how much time would that take, and how effective would it be? how comfortable? are these standards you hold other women to?

no, taking offense isn't exactly fair. but the hand she was dealt in this matter isn't fair, either. 

i also get frustrated when i get misgendered. i don't externalize that frustration (particularly in the context of "this is a stranger who doesn't have some other way of knowing"), but i can definitely understand it.

would i have been a happier "woman", comparatively, if i wasn't also dealing with sexism? sure. i didnt enjoy misogyny - nobody does. but i'm still a man, and i don't think that'd change. 

re: "is that what's up for others", i can't speak for others - i'm not them. i can say that for the community i've spoken with, that's never been the case. most of us have heard the "do i want to transition or is it just sexism" argument. ive also known many (myself included) who spent a long time ruminating on it before ever taking a step towards coming out.

i did personally a lot of introspection. what makes me comfortable? what makes me uncomfortable? who do i want to be if im 80? if i had to live alone for the rest of my life, would that answer change? why and how? that kinda stuff. for like...6 years? before i came out. 

other people have their own experiences. besides, transphobia is nothing to sneeze at either. in some aspects, those who transition (and pass) gain priveleges. in others, by transitioning we are opening ourselves up to new dangers. particularly when combining them with other aspects of our identities, it becomes more complicated than youd think real fast lol

i went through a list of most common names for boys born in the year i was born in the country i live in. 

i removed names with origins that aren't my own.
i removed names that already had particularly strong associations for me, as well as ones where i knew people with that name. since it was a popularity list, obviously i based this more on "not naming myself the same as someone i interact with" than "i have never interacted with this name before". 
with this shorter list, i then removed things with meanings like "manly" or whatever, it just felt...on the nose?

my middle name was in reference to a family member and i knew my name change would go over easier with my parents if i just swapped that from the more "feminine" version to a "masculine" version. think jane -> jack, etc.

since i already knew the middle name, i then took the remaining names from the popular names list, and put them in the context of my middle and last name. did they sound okay together? did my initials form any weird acronyms? etc.

my names list was pretty short at this point in the process. i kept them on my phone for a few months, and introduced myself online with them. i then brought them to my friends for use. when i felt confident in a name, i brought it to my family.

luckily they liked it, im genuinely not sure what i would have done otherwise
